comparisons.peer_summary: The allowance for credit losses is estimated using quantitative and qualitative methods, incorporating forward-looking macroeconomic scenarios such as GDP, unemployment, and real estate prices to determine the weighted economic outlook.

sentences.text: Under the base macroeconomic forecast as of 4Q24, U.S. real GDP growth is expected to slow during 2025 and 2026, while the unemployment rate is expected to increase in 2025, but decline in 2026.
• U.S. unemployment rate represents the rate forecasted as of the respective quarter-end.
• Growth in U.S. GDP represents the year-over-year growth rate forecasted for the respective years.

• While the U.S. unemployment and U.S. GDP growth rates are significant inputs to the forecast model, the model contemplates a variety of other inputs across a range of scenarios to provide a forecast of future economic conditions. Given the complex nature of the forecasting process, no single economic variable can be viewed in isolation and independently of other inputs.

comparisons.peer_summary: Qualitative adjustments included additional weight on adverse scenarios to reflect geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainties, using a weighted average of five internally developed macroeconomic scenarios where adverse scenarios incorporate more punitive factors than central case assumptions.
comparisons.comparison: Both companies incorporate macroeconomic scenarios, including adverse ones, into their credit loss estimates. Citi's base forecast anticipates a slowdown in GDP and a rise in unemployment in 2025, while JPMorgan's adverse scenarios assume a more punitive outcome with a U.S. unemployment rate peaking at 5.5% in Q4 2025 and real GDP being 1.9% lower than the central case by mid-2026. Both reflect concerns about economic downturns, though JPM explicitly weights additional uncertainty into adverse scenarios.

sentences.text: Under the base macroeconomic forecast as of 4Q24, U.S. real GDP growth is expected to slow during 2025 and 2026, while the unemployment rate is expected to increase in 2025, but decline in 2026.

The Firm's qualitative adjustments continued to include additional weight placed on the adverse scenarios to reflect ongoing uncertainties and downside risks related to the geopolitical and macroeconomic environment.
The adverse scenarios incorporate more punitive macroeconomic factors than the central case assumptions provided in the table below, resulting in:
• a weighted average U.S. unemployment rate peaking at 5.5% in the fourth quarter of 2025, and
• a weighted average U.S. real GDP level that is 1.9% lower than the central case at the end of the second quarter of 2026.
